title: Principles of Experimental Design
breadcrumb: Unit III · Design of Experiments · Core principles
objectives: Explain the principles of replication, randomisation and local control.
Distinguish experimental units, treatments, factors, blocks and replicates.
Explain how randomisation supports unbiased inference and valid error assessment.
Use local control/blocking to reduce nuisance variation.
Select CRD, RBD or Latin square according to the nuisance structure.

traps: Replication means independent experimental units receiving the same treatment, not repeated readings on one unit.
Randomisation is used to protect against systematic allocation bias and justify probability-based error assessment.
Local control reduces nuisance variation by grouping similar units into blocks.
Blocking is not the same as replication: a block controls a nuisance source; replication supplies repeated treatment applications.
CRD uses no blocking; RBD controls one major nuisance direction; Latin square controls two orthogonal directions.
Randomisation does not guarantee equal group sizes or remove all confounding by itself.
A design principle is not a specific layout: replication, randomisation and local control work together.
howto: Identify the experimental unit and treatment structure first. Replicate treatments on independent units, randomise allocation within the restrictions of the design, and use blocks when a known nuisance source creates systematic variation. Choose CRD, RBD or Latin square from the number and structure of nuisance directions.

sheet: Replication: apply each treatment to multiple independent experimental units.
Randomisation: allocate treatments using a chance mechanism.
Local control: group similar units into blocks to reduce nuisance variation.
Replication estimates experimental error and improves precision.
Randomisation protects against allocation bias and supports valid inference.
Blocking explains systematic nuisance variation rather than leaving it in residual error.
CRD: no blocks; RBD: one blocking factor; Latin square: row and column blocking.
Blocks must be formed before treatment allocation; randomise treatments within the permitted structure.
Repeated measurements on one unit are not automatically independent replicates.
cards: Smallest unit independently assigned a treatment

tricks.why: Independent experimental units, not merely repeated readings.
Group units that are alike on a nuisance variable.

shortcuts: Ask what is replicated: the experimental unit, not the observation count.
Ask how many nuisance directions are controlled: zero, one or two.
Randomise within the restrictions imposed by the chosen layout.
remember: The three principles are complementary, not alternatives.
Blocking reduces nuisance variation; randomisation protects unbiased comparisons.
traps: Treating blocking and randomisation as interchangeable.

scenes.title: What makes an experiment well designed?
scenes.objective: Identify the role of design before data collection.
body: An experiment compares treatments by assigning them to experimental units and measuring responses. The design specifies which units receive which treatments and how assignment is carried out.
A sound design protects comparisons from systematic bias, provides a basis for estimating experimental error, and controls known nuisance variation where possible.

items.ask: What is the purpose of experimental design?
items.recall: Plan treatment allocation so comparisons are fair, precise and interpretable.
refresh: Define the experimental unit before counting observations.
Allocation determines which treatment is applied to which unit.
Good design supports valid estimation and inference.

scenes.title: Fisher's three principles
scenes.objective: Name and distinguish replication, randomisation and local control.
body: The classical principles are replication, randomisation and local control (often implemented through blocking). They address different needs: repeated independent applications, chance allocation, and control of nuisance heterogeneity.
They work together. A design may replicate and randomise while also blocking units that share a known nuisance condition.

scenario.teaser: A field trial compares four fertilisers across a sloping field.
scenario.title: Identify the three principles
body: Each fertiliser is applied to several separate plots (replication). Fertilisers are assigned by a random procedure (randomisation). Similar plots are grouped into blocks along the slope (local control).
The slope is a nuisance source because it may affect yield independently of fertiliser.
scenario.q: Which principle is implemented by grouping similar plots?

ask.q: Name the three classical principles of experimental design.
ask.nudge: One repeats, one uses chance, one controls nuisance variation.

blocks.body: The experimental unit is the smallest unit independently assigned to a treatment. It may be a plot, patient, animal, batch or machine.
Replication applies the same treatment to multiple independent experimental units. It provides information about experimental variability and improves precision.
Several measurements on one treated unit are subsamples or repeated measurements, not automatically independent replications. Treating them as independent can underestimate uncertainty.

ask.q: If one plot is measured five times, how many independently treated plots have been replicated?
ask.nudge: Repeated readings do not create new experimental units.

scenes.title: Count the experimental units
scenes.objective: Calculate units from treatments and replication.
scenes.problem: A completely randomised experiment compares five treatments with four independent units per treatment. How many experimental units are required?
hints: Multiply treatment count by independent replicates per treatment.

solution.math: There are 20 independently treated experimental units.

scenes.check: Five treatments each applied to four independent units.

ask.q: Six treatments with three independent replicates each require how many units?

scenes.title: Randomisation protects comparisons
scenes.objective: Explain why chance allocation is essential.

blocks.body: Randomisation assigns treatments to experimental units using a chance mechanism, subject to the restrictions of the design.
It prevents investigators from systematically assigning favourable units to preferred treatments and supports probability-based inference under the model.
Randomisation does not guarantee identical groups, eliminate all variation, or repair a fundamentally unsuitable design. It protects against systematic allocation bias in expectation.

ask.q: Does randomisation guarantee exactly equal baseline characteristics in every realised experiment?
ask.nudge: Think about what chance allocation guarantees in expectation, not in every sample.

scenes.title: Local control: block similar units
body: Local control groups experimental units that are similar with respect to a known nuisance variable, such as soil fertility, operator, batch or day. Treatments are then compared within these relatively homogeneous groups.
Blocking accounts for systematic nuisance variation and can reduce residual error, increasing precision of treatment comparisons when blocks are effective.

scenario.teaser: A field has a fertility gradient from north to south.
scenario.title: Use blocks to control the gradient
body: If the gradient is ignored, one fertiliser may receive more fertile plots by chance or through poor allocation. Divide the field into blocks of nearby, similar plots and randomise all treatments within each block when using a complete RBD.
The block effect is separated from treatment variation in the analysis.
scenario.q: What nuisance source is local control addressing?

ask.q: What is the main statistical purpose of blocking?
ask.nudge: Move predictable nuisance variation out of residual error.

scenes.title: Replication, randomisation and blocking are not substitutes

blocks.body: Replication asks whether treatments are applied to multiple independent units. Randomisation asks how assignments are chosen. Blocking asks whether similar units should be grouped to control a nuisance source.
An RBD can replicate treatments across blocks, randomise treatments within each block, and use blocks for local control. The principles complement one another.

ask.q: Which principle controls a known soil gradient by grouping similar plots?

scenes.title: Choose CRD, RBD or Latin square
scenes.objective: Match design layout to nuisance structure.
scenes.problem: A laboratory compares five treatments. Units are homogeneous and no important blocking variable is identified. Which basic design is suitable?
hints: Ask whether nuisance grouping is needed.

solution.math: A randomised block design (RBD) would control one blocking direction.

solution.say: If two orthogonal nuisance factors existed.
solution.math: A Latin square could control row and column effects, subject to its structural restrictions.

scenes.answer: CRD is appropriate when units are sufficiently homogeneous and no blocking factor is needed.
scenes.check: CRD has no explicit blocks; RBD has one; Latin square has two.

ask.q: A trial has one known nuisance gradient. Which common design controls it?

blocks.body: In a CRD, treatment labels are randomly allocated across all experimental units.
In a complete RBD, treatments are randomly permuted within each block so every treatment appears once per block.
A Latin square requires randomisation that preserves one occurrence of each treatment in every row and column; arbitrary independent assignment would destroy the layout.

ask.q: In a complete RBD, where are treatments randomised?

blocks.body: Precision concerns the variability of an estimator. Effective replication and blocking can reduce uncertainty.
Randomisation protects against systematic allocation bias; it does not guarantee a small standard error.
A well-randomised experiment can still have limited generalisability if units, settings or treatment implementation do not represent the target population.

ask.q: Does a precise experiment automatically guarantee broad generalisability?
ask.nudge: Internal design quality and external validity are different.

scenes.title: Diagnose common design mistakes
scenes.problem: A researcher applies three treatments to one plot each, measures every plot ten times, and assigns the preferred treatment to the best-looking plot.

solution.math: There is only one independently treated plot per treatment; ten readings do not create ten independent plots.
Assigning the preferred treatment to the best-looking plot is systematic allocation, not randomisation.
If plots differ along a known gradient, use blocks of similar plots and randomise within blocks.

scenes.answer: The study lacks independent replication and randomisation; blocking may also be needed.
scenes.check: Independent units, chance allocation and nuisance control are distinct.

ask.q: What is wrong with treating ten readings on one plot as ten replicates?
ask.nudge: The treatment was assigned only once to that plot.

traps.q: Are repeated readings on one unit automatically replication?
traps.a: No; independent experimental units are required.

traps.q: Does randomisation guarantee equal group means?
traps.a: No; it protects against systematic allocation bias in expectation.
No; treatments are randomised within the blocks.

traps.q: How many nuisance directions does an ordinary RBD control?

scenes.title: Select a design from the nuisance pattern
scenes.problem: A crop experiment has two identifiable nuisance directions: a north–south fertility gradient and an east–west irrigation gradient. A Latin square layout is feasible and treatment count matches rows and columns. Which design principle is being used?
hints: Two orthogonal nuisance directions are present.
Local control is implemented in rows and columns.

solution.math: A Latin square controls row and column effects, with each treatment appearing once in every row and column.

scenes.answer: Local control through a Latin square design.
scenes.check: The design controls two orthogonal nuisance factors.

ask.q: Which design controls two orthogonal blocking directions?

scenes.title: Principles mastery checkpoint
scenes.objective: Consolidate the three principles and their use.
body: Replication uses multiple independent experimental units; randomisation uses chance allocation; local control groups similar units to reduce nuisance variation.
CRD has no explicit blocking, RBD controls one blocking factor, and Latin square controls two orthogonal directions. The principles complement each other and do not eliminate all error.
